newsitem.title: USA: Florida hospitals see bigger profit margins -- study.
newsitem.headline: Florida hospitals see bigger profit margins -- study.

text.p: Florida hospitals saw their average profit margin rise to 5.5 percent in 1995 from 3.3 percent in 1991, according to a study by Florida Hospital Association.
The study used data submitted to Florida Agency for Health Care Administration. It did not separate the data to compare private, for-profit hospitals against public hospitals.
The overall health of Florida hospitals has improved, with only 39 losing money in 1995, compared to 63 in 1991.

Net revenues received by Florida hospitals grew to $15 billion in 1995, up 24 percent from 1991. But expenses grew by only 22 percent during the period, reflecting efficiency and cost containment efforts, the report said.
Operating margin, income from patient care servics, rose to 3.3 percent in 1995 from 1.4 percent in 1991.

But as Florida's population ages, more and more of its hospitals are becoming predominently Medicare hospitals. In 1995, 85 of the state's 202 hospitals, or 42 percent, had more than 65 percent of their patient-days from Medicare.
Medicare accounted for 45 percent of Florida hospital revenues but consumed almost 50 percent of the resources in 1995.
The data reflect a growing trend toward managed care among private patients. Managed care accounted for 27 percent of revenues and 19 percent of patient days in 1995.
The study documented a trend toward shorter but more intensive hospital stays, and increased use of outpatient services.
The average length of stay declined by 16 percent, to 5.6 days in 1995 from 6.7 days in 1991, while revenues and costs on an adjusted patient-day basis continued to rise.
Outpatient revenue represent a growing proportion of hospital services, accounting for 28 percent of revenues in 1995. That was up from 22 percent in 1991.

The volume of charity care declined slightly between 1991 and 1995, possibly reflecting tightened criteria used to classify patients as needy. Bad debt increased steadily during the period, reflecting an increase in the uninsured population and patients' inability to pay higher copayments and deductibles, the study said.
Salaries remained the biggest expense, representing 40 percent of hospital costs. Despite cost-cutting efforts, staffing rose to 4.93 full-time employees per hospital bed in 1995, from 4.8 in 1991.
